div.head: III Eg 4
div.ab: ⁊ se þe oðerne mid wóge forseggan wille, þæt he aþor oððe feo oððe feore þe wyrsa sý, gyf þonne se oðer geunsoðian mæge, þæt him man onsecgan wolde, si he his tungan scyldig, butan he hine mid his were forgylde.

⁊ se ðe oðerne mid wó forsecgan wille, þæt he aðer oððe feo oððe feore (uel freme) þe wyrsa sy, gif þonne se oðer þæt geunsoðian mæge, þæt him mon onsecgan wolde, sy he his tungan scyldig, buton he hine mid his were forgylde.

And se þe oðerne mid woge forseccan wille, þæt he aðor oððe feo oððe freme þe wyrsa sy, gif þonne se oðer þæt geunsoðian mæge, þæt him man onsecgan wolde, sy he his tungan scildig, buton he hine mid his were forgilde.

⁊ se þe oþerne mid wó forsecgan wille, þæt he aðer oððe feo oþþe freme þe wyrse sy, gyf þonne se oðer þæt geunsoðian mæge, þæt him man onsecgan wolde, sy he his tungan scyldig, buton he hine mid his were forgylde.
Et qui aliquem iniuste superdicere presumet, unde uita uel commodo peior sit, lingue sue reus erit, si accusatus se idoneare et accusationem falsare poterit, nisi se redimat wera sua.

[Be ðon ðe mon oþerne forsecgaþ.] And se þe oðerne mid woge forseccan wille, þæt he aðor oððe feo oððe freme þe wyrsa sy, gif þonne se oðer þæt geunsoðian mæge þæt him man onsecgan wolde, sy he his tungan scildig, buton he hine mid his were forgilde.

And se þe oðerne mid woge forseggan wille þæt he aþor oððe feo oððe feore þe wyrsa sy, gyf þonne se oðer geunsoðian mæge, þæt him man onsecgan wolde, si he his tungan scyldig butan he hine mid his were forgylde.

(Davon, dass jemand einen verleumdet. Ld) Und wer einen andern mit Bosheit verklagen will, so dass dieser entweder an Gut oder Leben (Gedeihen A D G2) dadurch geschädigt wird: wenn dann der andere [Verklagte] als unwahr erweisen kann, was jener über ihn klagen wollte, so sei jener seine Zunge [zu verlieren] schuldig, ausser wenn er sich durch sein Wergeld auslöst.

(Of slandering someone. Ld) And whoever wishes to accuse another maliciously, so that the latter is harmed thereby either in property or in life (prosperity, A D G2): if the other [accused] can then prove false what that man wished to charge him with, let that man be liable [to lose] his tongue, unless he redeems himself with his wergild.

And if anyone seeks to accuse another man falsely, so that he is injured either in property or in reputation, and if the second man can refute the charge which the first has sought to bring against him, the first shall forfeit his tongue, unless he redeem himself with his wergeld.

And he who wishes to accuse another falsely, so that he suffer loss either of property or of life, if the other can then prove what one would charge him with to be false, he [the accuser] is to forfeit his tongue, unless he redeem himself with his wergild.

And if anyone who seeks to bring a false charge against another so that he is the worse in either property or well-being, and if the accused can disprove the charge that has been brought against him, then the accuser shall lose his tongue unless he can redeem himself through the payment of his wergild.

feorh hinter feo bildet vielfach ein Paar der Alliteration; s. d. Wb; vgl. Ann. Anglosax. zu 755. Auch dem Sinne entspricht feorh, da zunächst Leibesstrafe den in Kriminalklage Überführten, so den am häufigsten vorkommenden handhaften Diebstahl, bedrohte. Auch ist fremu dem feo zu sinnverwandt, dass anzunehmen wäre, Eadgar habe daraus eine besondere Schadensklasse gebildet. Richtig also (o. Erkl. 1) steht vita in Hn 34, 7.—Wohl ursprünglich nur am Rande stand freme laut Q schon in Rec. I und, laut der anderen Hss., in Rec. II, der Cnut folgt. Eine zweite Verderbnis setzt feorm in Cnut Hs. A gemäss der o. I 400† zitierten Formel

feorh after feo frequently forms an alliterative pair; see that word in Wb; cf. Ann. Anglosax. under 755. feorh also fits the sense, since corporal punishment threatened primarily the man convicted on a criminal charge, for instance of theft caught in the act, the most frequent case. Moreover fremu is too close in meaning to feo for it to be supposed that Eadgar made of it a separate class of damage. vita in Hn 34, 7 (above note 1) is therefore correct. — freme, probably at first only in the margin, already stood in Rec. I, as Q shows, and, as the other MSS show, in Rec. II, which Cnut follows. A second corruption puts feorm in Cnut MS A, in accordance with the formula cited above I 400†
Also strenger als Af 32; vgl. Gl Zunge 3. Nicht etwa des Verletzten Wergeld, wie Moeller Wergeld 43 meint
Thus stricter than Af 32; cf. Gl Zunge 3. Not, say, the injured man’s wergild, as Moeller Wergeld 43 thinks

There is a curious discrepancy in regard to the reading—a discrepancy which seems to be independent of the general relationship of the MSS. All the texts have feo but A, G have feore (vel freme being written above in A) against D, G₂ with freme, while Q has vita vel commodo, i.e. feore oððe freme. In II Cn. 16 all the A.S. texts have feo, A has feorme, B frema, Ld feorh, but Q here has pecunia vel commodo, i.e. feo oððe freme. Hn. 34, 7 has vitae iacturam vel honoris detrimentum, i.e. feore oððe freme. Liebermann thinks that the original reading in Edgar’s law was probably feore, partly because the phrase feo oððe feore occurs in E. and G. 12; VIII Atr. 33; II Cn. 40 and Sax. Chr. ann. 755, and partly because freme is too near in meaning to feo, but the reading feorh may very well have been taken from E. and G. 12 and the other passages in the Laws in which the reference is not to slander but to robbery or murder, while Hn. 34, 7 makes it clear that freme was understood as referring to ‘honour’ and not to property, cf. Norse rett, Irish ‘honour-price,’ and Welsh saraad, Seebohm, Tribal Custom in A.S. Law, p. 240.

note.label: life
note.seg: The reading of the full version in Nero. The Harley MS. writes vel freme over feore “life”, while Corpus and the Wulfstan version in Nero replace feore by freme. This word means “benefit”, though “reputation”, recorded after the Conquest, is possible. Instead of “property or life” Quadripartitus has uita uel commodo. In one group of the MSS of Wulfstan’s “Sermon of the Wolf to the English” (No. 240, p. 930, n. 4) one gets: ge æt freme ge æt fostre ge æt feo ge æt feore.
